reconcile.connective: JFB treats Rahab's "works" not as a rival ground of salvation but as faith itself made visible — the very thing Hebrews already credits to her faith.

discrepancy.connective: Martin Luther pressed this as genuine: his 1522 Preface to the Epistle of James pronounced it "flatly against St. Paul ... in ascribing justification to works" — the charge covering Rahab's verdict too.

skeptic.name: Martin Luther
skeptic.work: Preface to the Epistle of James (1522)
skeptic.attribution: Martin Luther (1483-1546), Preface to the Epistle of James (1522)

excerpts.excerpt_text: It is clear from the nature of Rahab's act, that it is not quoted to prove justification by works as such. … Hence Heb 11:31 names this as an example of faith, rather than of obedience. … The nature of the works alleged is such as to prove that James uses them only as evidences of faith, as contrasted with a mere verbal profession: not works of charity and piety, but works the value of which consisted solely in their being proofs of faith: they were faith expressed in act, synonymous with faith itself.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB explicitly cross-references Heb 11:31 and Jas 2:25 as the same episode, arguing James's 'works' are evidentiary proof of the very faith Hebrews attributes to Rahab, not a rival cause of salvation.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible, note on James 2:14 (1706-14)
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry devotes an extended excursus at James 2:14 to reconciling Paul and James on faith and works, explicitly naming Rahab (Jas 2:25) as the second proof-text alongside Abraham; Haley's Discrepancies treats only the separate 'did Rahab lie' question and does not cover this faith/works pairing, so the row-surfaced harmonizing commentator is used instead.
